title: Fix a hook tight to a hollow wall with its toggle bolt
instruction: Fix the hook tight against the wall, square to the pencil line.
context: General maintenance and repair workers (about 1.5 million in the US) hang hooks, brackets and fixtures on hollow walls with spring-wing toggle bolts. The usual way this job fails is the toggle spinning in the cavity: the nut behind the board cannot be reached, and the screw then turns without drawing the hook tight.
setup: Positions from the robot's view: 'in front' is the distance ahead of the line through the two arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the midline halfway between them, heights are above the table top. Wall (fixed): a section of installed hollow wall standing upright on the table, its face toward the robot 28.0 cm in front, 20.5 cm wide (from 19.5 cm right to 1.0 cm left) and 30 cm tall: a wooden 2x3 frame (bottom plate on the table, top plate and two studs, 38 mm thick and 63.5 mm deep) with grey 12.7 mm wallboard on both sides, so the 63.5 mm cavity inside is closed. A prepared hole 12.7 mm across goes through the front board 6.0 cm right and 15.0 cm up. A pencil line 3 mm wide runs plumb (straight down) the face through the hole's centre. Hook (loose, steel, 150 g): a flat plate 40 mm wide, 125 mm tall and 3 mm thick hanging against the face along the line, with an 8 mm round arm 80 mm below the bolt standing straight out 75 mm from the plate, its end turned up to 14 mm above the arm's centre line. Toggle bolt: a 3/16 in (10-24) x 2-1/2 in machine screw (4.8 mm, 1.06 mm per turn) with a zinc hex washer head (a 5/16 in, 7.9 mm hex 2.4 mm tall on a washer face 10.3 mm across and 0.6 mm thick), through the plate 40 mm below its top and through the hole, resting on the hole's bottom (the hook hangs flat on the face, 3.7 mm low). On it in the cavity, the spring-wing toggle nut with its wings opened: 48 mm across (level), 11 mm wide and 6 mm thick, its front face 3 mm behind the front board's back (about 2.8 turns of thread to take up). Nut driver (loose, 90 g): a stubby ratcheting 5/16 in nut driver, 92 mm long: red handle 35 mm across and 50 mm long with a black cap, a 6 mm shaft 28 mm long and a steel socket 13 mm across and 10 mm long whose bore, 10 mm across and 4 mm deep with a 45 degree lead-in opening it to 12 mm at the mouth, fits over the hex and stops on the washer face. The ratchet drives clockwise (seen from the handle) and freewheels anticlockwise. It stands socket-down in a holder: a fixed black block 50 x 50 x 45 mm centred 17.0 cm in front and 24.0 cm right, with a 14 mm vertical bore; the handle rests on the block's top. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Judged at the end, with no gripper within 5 mm of the hook and the nut driver (put down or held) at least 5 mm from it. Flush: a 1 mm feeler gauge cannot go under any edge of the plate. Tug test, run by the scorer once the robot has handled the hook and let it go, and it is flush, within 10 degrees of plumb and still for 1 s: a spring scale hooked on the hook's arm pulls 20 N straight out from the wall for 0.5 s, then lets off for 0.5 s. Tight: during the tug no edge of the plate comes 1 mm off the wall (the gauge still cannot go in), and afterwards both ends of the plate are within 1 mm of where they were (pencil ticks at its ends). Anything touching or moving the hook restarts the test. Square: the plate's long edge within 3 degrees of the pencil line (a protractor), hook end down. 1.0: tight and square. 0.5: tight, 3 to 10 degrees off. 0 otherwise: loose (an unclamped hook comes off the wall under the tug), not flush, more than 10 degrees off, upside down, a gripper or the nut driver within 5 mm, or no finished test.
reset_notes: 1. Unscrew the bolt (anticlockwise) until the wings are 3 mm behind the front board, about 2.8 turns from tight; the toggle spins unless the hook is pulled out from the wall while turning, so hold it out while unscrewing. 2. Let the hook hang on its bolt, plate against the face along the pencil line, hook end down, the wings level. 3. Stand the nut driver socket-down in its holder's bore. Nothing is consumed.
fidelity: True size; a short section of an installed wall, upright on the bench, the hole low on it. The thread is an ideal 1.06 mm/turn joint; a stop keeps it from backing off. The socket's grip on the hex is a rule: seated, it turns the screw and takes the equal reaction (up to 0.35 N m); once snug, thread friction takes 0.3 N m of it. A tight hook's plate edge came 0.28 to 0.35 mm off the springy board under the 20 N tug. Fixed layout.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (2 trials, --epochs 2; the arms moved toward the wall and the nut driver but nothing was picked up and the hook was not touched); demo: 1.0 (2 trials, --epochs 2; each passed the 20 N tug test, the plate edge 0.28 and 0.35 mm off the face, 0.0 and 0.1 degrees off plumb)
